source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
finding: Proposes that people judge probability and value with a few heuristics: representativeness, availability, and adjustment and anchoring. They are usually useful but cause systematic errors.
numbers: Three heuristics named: representativeness, availability, anchoring and adjustment.
limits: Descriptive claim. No process model and little control data. Later critics call the heuristics vague.
agent_relevance: Names the error families our schema must expect from a fast answer: similarity over base rate, ease over frequency, first number over evidence.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
finding: Base-rate neglect with worthless evidence. Subjects given a bland description (Dick) judged P(engineer)=.5 whether the group was 70% or 30% engineers. With no description they used the prior correctly.
numbers: Judged probability .5 in both the .7 and .3 conditions.
quote: people respond differently when given no evidence and when given worthless evidence
limits: Authors say the description was meant to carry no information. Many later variants exist.
agent_relevance: An agent should not let an added detail replace a stated prior. Code can compare answers across prior values (a mutated input, G3).

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
finding: Insensitivity to sample size, hospital problem: larger hospital about 45 births a day, smaller about 15. Which records more days with over 60% boys?
numbers: Answers: larger 21, smaller 21, about the same (within 5%) 53, from undergraduate students. Correct answer: the smaller hospital.
limits: Student sample, counts only. Wording and frequency format change rates in later work.
agent_relevance: Same item used on GPT-3 by Binz and Schulz (2022). A cheap check for sample-size neglect in a model.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
finding: Misconceptions of chance and of regression. H-T-H-T-T-H judged likelier than H-H-H-T-T-T because it looks random; gambler's fallacy; predicting a remote criterion exactly as the input is evaluated.
numbers: Student-teacher study: percentile predictions of success 5 years later were identical to percentile evaluations of the practice lesson.
limits: Authors argue people never learn regression from everyday experience.
agent_relevance: Predictions from weak evidence should be shrunk toward a base rate. A program step can enforce shrinking by count.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
finding: Availability by imaginability. Subjects estimated how many committees of 2 versus 8 can be formed from 10 people. Small committees are easier to construct so seem more numerous.
numbers: Median estimate for 2-member committees 70, for 8-member committees 20. Correct answer is 45 for both.
limits: Shows ease of construction drives frequency judgment. Does not separate ease from content of recall.
agent_relevance: LLMs judge frequency from how readily an example comes. Get counts from code or retrieval, not from recall feel.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
finding: Anchoring on a random number: a number was set in the subjects' presence, then they judged the percentage of African countries in the UN.
numbers: Median estimates 25 for the group given anchor 10 and 45 for the group given anchor 65.
limits: Authors report the effect was not removed by payoffs for accuracy. Mechanism (adjustment versus selective priming) was later disputed.
agent_relevance: Any number in the prompt can pull the answer. Strip irrelevant numbers; do not show a prior answer before a fresh estimate.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
finding: Insufficient adjustment in a computation task: estimate 8x7x6x5x4x3x2x1 or the reverse order within 5 seconds.
numbers: Median 512 for the ascending order and 2,250 for the descending order. Correct is 40,320.
limits: Speeded estimation; shows anchoring on the first steps.
agent_relevance: Stepwise model reasoning also anchors on early steps; let code do the arithmetic.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
finding: Overconfidence in subjective probability distributions, and anchoring on stated odds. Subjects' 98% intervals were too narrow.
numbers: True value fell outside the 1st to 99th percentile interval in about 30 percent of problems (should be 2 percent). Group 2 odds on stated values: median 3:1 instead of 9:1; events given .34 average probability occurred 26 percent of the time.
limits: Early calibration data; later work (hard-easy effect, elicitation format) qualifies it.
agent_relevance: Stated confidence from the model must be checked against outcomes by code, never trusted.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
finding: Conjunctive and disjunctive events: people overestimate conjunctions (plans succeed) and underestimate disjunctions, by anchoring on the single-step probability. Bar-Hillel gambles: most subjects bet on the conjunctive event over the simple one and on the simple one over the disjunctive one.
numbers: Conjunctive event (7 reds in a row from 90% red bag) has probability .48, lower than the simple 50% event, yet most subjects preferred it.
limits: Basis of the planning fallacy account.
agent_relevance: Multi-step plans need a program that multiplies step probabilities; do not let the model estimate the product.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1981) The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice
finding: Asian disease problem: the same outcomes described as lives saved or lives lost flip choice from risk averse to risk seeking.
numbers: Problem 1 (N=152): 72% chose sure 200 saved, 28% the 1/3 chance of saving 600. Problem 2 (N=155): 22% chose sure 400 die, 78% chose the 2/3 chance that 600 die.
limits: Authors report it in faculty and physicians too. Size depends on wording in later work.
agent_relevance: The same facts in different words must give the same answer. Re-ask in the other frame and compare in code.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1981) The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice
finding: Dominance violation from narrow framing: two decisions presented together were chosen as sure gain plus a risky loss, a dominated combination.
numbers: Problem 3 (N=150): 84% chose sure gain $240; 87% chose the 75% chance to lose 1000. 73% picked A and D; 3% picked B and C. Combined in problem 4 (N=86), 100% chose the dominant option.
limits: Authors say real payoffs gave a similar pattern.
agent_relevance: An agent that settles sub-decisions one by one can pick a dominated whole. Combine the options in code first.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1981) The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice
finding: Pseudocertainty and mental accounting: the same economics flips with the framing of the account.
numbers: Problem 5 (N=77): 78% sure $30. Problem 6 (N=85, two-stage game): 74% sure $30. Calculator: 68% would drive for $5 off a $15 calculator, 29% off a $125 one (N=93 and N=88).
limits: Hypothetical choices from students; some problems paid 1 in 10.
agent_relevance: Equal gains should count equally; relative framing is a check item in cost choices.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1983) Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: the conjunction fallacy
finding: Linda problem: most people rank 'bank teller and feminist' above 'bank teller', breaking the rule that a conjunction cannot exceed its parts.
numbers: The 85% choosing the conjunction is quoted in Suri et al. (2023), which I opened. I did not open the 1983 paper.
limits: Not opened. Rates fall with frequency format and with reading 'probable' strictly.
agent_relevance: A rule code can check on any answer: P(A and B) must not exceed P(A).

source: Kahneman & Frederick (2002) Representativeness revisited: attribute substitution in intuitive judgment
finding: Updated theory: facing a hard target question, people answer an easier related one (the heuristic attribute) unless System 2 monitoring catches it. It unifies representativeness, availability and affect.
numbers: No figures recorded.
limits: Not opened; from background knowledge. Hard to falsify; does not say when System 2 intervenes.
agent_relevance: Fits LLMs well: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) test substitution directly with name versus description conflicts.

source: Gigerenzer (1996) On narrow norms and vague heuristics; Kahneman & Tversky (1996) On the reality of cognitive illusions
finding: Main rival view. Gigerenzer says the heuristics are vague labels, the norms narrow, and errors shrink with natural frequencies. Kahneman and Tversky reply that errors remain across many tasks.
numbers: No figures recorded.
limits: Not opened; from background knowledge.
agent_relevance: Pose probability problems as counts instead of percentages, and test whether answers improve.

source: Klein et al. (2014) Investigating variation in replicability: a Many Labs replication project
finding: Multi-site replication of 13 classic effects. Anchoring and gain-loss framing were reported as replicating; two priming effects were not.
numbers: No effect sizes recorded; the page returned 403.
limits: Not opened; from background knowledge, count unverified.
agent_relevance: Anchoring and framing are the safest effects to build tests on.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 chose the conjunction in the Linda problem, avoided base-rate neglect in the cab problem, and missed the hospital sample-size problem, like people.
numbers: 12 of 12 standard vignettes answered correctly or human-like. All three CRT items: the intuitive wrong answer. Prospect-theory pairs: framing, certainty and probability-weighting shown, 3 of 6 effects.
limits: GPT-3 only. Small adversarial wording changes produced non-human mistakes, so success may be memory of known tasks.
agent_relevance: Vignette results may reflect training memory. Our tests must use new mutated problems (G3).

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models
finding: Early GPT-3 models fall for CRT and semantic-illusion traps like people. ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 mostly avoid them. Chain of thought helps weaker models.
numbers: 150 CRT tasks. Humans 38% correct vs 41% in original (n=3,428). davinci-003: 5% correct, 80% intuitive. ChatGPT-3.5: 59% correct, 15% intuitive. ChatGPT-4: 96% correct, 0% intuitive. Chain of thought on davinci-003: correct 5% to 28%, intuitive 80% to 29%.
limits: Bespoke tasks, not original wording. ChatGPT-4 stays high with chain of thought blocked (95% to 88%), so it may have memorised the type.
agent_relevance: Newer models do not show the human bias on known traps. Chain of thought still cuts bias in weaker models.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models
finding: Worked examples of the same CRT task type with the correct answer raise correct answers step by step: intuition can be trained in context.
numbers: 0 to 49 solved examples before each task; fastest gains on CRT Type 2.
limits: Same task type as the examples; transfer to new tasks untested.
agent_relevance: Few-shot examples of the right habit may help, but the gain is task-bound.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models
finding: When chain of thought is suppressed by instruction, ChatGPT-3.5 accuracy does not change, which fits memorised or learned intuition rather than written reasoning doing the work.
numbers: Chain-of-thought share fell from 97% to 0% for ChatGPT-3.5; correct answers changed by 4% (p=.49). ChatGPT-4 correct fell 95% to 88%.
limits: Interpretive; contamination also fits.
agent_relevance: Written reasoning is not a reliable record of why the model answered; supports checking by code.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee & Nguyen (2023) Do LLMs show decision heuristics similar to humans?
finding: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) was moved by random anchors, picked a conjunction, and showed framing and endowment effects, like human participants.
numbers: Anchoring: ChatGPT low-anchor mean 20.83 vs humans 22.5; high-anchor 105.97 vs 80.50 (60 humans, 30 per cell). Conjunction: ChatGPT 18 of 20, humans 10 of 20. Endowment: ChatGPT kept the old coin in 37 of 40 trials (92.5%), humans 34 of 40 (85%).
limits: Small cells, custom prompts. The original Linda error disappeared after a public post, probably through RLHF updates.
agent_relevance: Bias behaviour changes between releases. Rerun bias tests for each model version.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee & Nguyen (2023) Do LLMs show decision heuristics similar to humans?
finding: Framing: the model rated a medicine as more efficacious when described positively. Authors suggest language itself may be a source of these effects.
numbers: Mean efficacy rating 5.2 (positive frame) vs 4.6 (negative frame) in the model, confidence intervals not overlapping.
limits: Interpretation, not a test; imitation of training text also fits.
agent_relevance: Weakens the claim that biases need affect or effort. A prompt-level fix may work since the pull is textual.

source: Itzhak, Stanovsky, Rosenfeld & Belinkov (2023) Instructed to Bias
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF make models more biased on decoy, certainty and belief-bias tasks than the base model.
numbers: Bias score = target choice rate under treatment minus control. Certainty effect: davinci-002 0.24, davinci-003 0.67. Belief bias (invalid): davinci-002 0.55, davinci-003 0.65. Mistral base 0.05 vs Mistral-Instruct 0.26. GPT-4 certainty 0.15, belief valid 0.41.
limits: Some base models show negative decoy scores from always picking the last option: a position bias.
agent_relevance: More alignment training does not mean less bias. Test the exact model we use.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley & He (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: A 13,465-prompt admissions set covers prompt-induced, sequential and inherent biases. A self-help prompt where the model debiases its own prompt works better than hand-built examples.
numbers: GPT-4 admitted 40.5% more students under the reject framing than the admit framing. Llama-2 7B classified 32.1% fewer females as good at math. Anchoring self-help: Llama models changed 40 to 52% of decisions. Self-help left 0% (Llama-2 13B) and 1.4% (7B) biased framing prompts; GPT-4 2.7%.
limits: No clear status quo bias. Few-shot mitigation sometimes drove admission rate to 0 or 1.
agent_relevance: One review pass can help, but flips of 40-52% show it is noisy; use it only on a signal (G1).

source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases
finding: Uses framing, anchoring, availability and attribute substitution to predict failures of Codex and CodeGen.
numbers: Framing line copied: Codex 81% vs 4.5% baseline; CodeGen 70.7% vs 0.0%. Name-description conflict: Codex accuracy falls from 100% to 4.4-4.6%. Availability: accuracy falls from 50% to 17% when the operation order is flipped.
limits: Code models only, older Codex.
agent_relevance: Tests substitution directly. A program should check that name and description agree before code runs.

source: Macmillan-Scott & Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and Cognitive Biases in Large Language Models
finding: Seven LLMs on 12 classic tasks. They are inconsistent, and most wrong answers are not the human bias but plain illogic.
numbers: Correct with sound reasoning: GPT-4 69.2%, Claude 2 55.0%. Llama-2 7B wrong in 77.5%. Human-like wrong: GPT-3.5 21.7% (50.8% counting human-like correct); GPT-4 human-like 73.3%; Llama-2 13B 8.3%. Llama-2 70B refused in 41.7%.
limits: Default settings, few runs per task; tasks may be in training data.
agent_relevance: Model errors do not follow the human bias catalogue, so guardrails must not rely on human bias lists alone.

source: Shaki, Kraus & Wooldridge (2023) Cognitive Effects in Large Language Models
finding: Five cognitive effects tested on text-davinci-003 using token-probability confidence. Priming, distance, SNARC and size congruity found; anchoring absent.
numbers: Anchoring not found, in contrast to Suri et al.
limits: Used probability confidence, a different measure from choice tasks.
agent_relevance: Anchoring in LLMs depends on method. Measure it in our own pipeline.

source: Koo et al. (2024) Benchmarking Cognitive Biases in LLMs as Evaluators (COBBLER)
finding: Six biases (order, compassion fade, egocentric, salience, bandwagon, attentional) in 16 LLM judges. Most models are strongly biased.
numbers: 16 models, 50 instructions, 42K samples per bias set (630K total), 300 human annotations. The largest models prefer their own answers above 50% when names are hidden; larger models favour longer answers.
limits: Measures judge bias against a random baseline, not intuitive error.
agent_relevance: Supports our rule that the model does not grade its own answer.
